children: Investors pounced on rising rates, buying 10-year Treasury notes at the highest yield achieved at an auction in 19 years.

Investors absorbed $39 billion worth of 10-year notes auctioned at 1 pm. While the yield achieved was 4.834%, the highest level at any 10-year auction since August 2007, this was a reflection of ongoing market dynamics. The bid/cover ratio was 2.71, meaning $2.71 in bids were received for every $1 of debt on offer, which is stronger than the average ratio of 2.52 for similar auctions.

Yields on longer-duration bonds have been rising thanks to strong economic growth, inflation fears, and growing borrowing needs from the U.S. government. While Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has endeavored to keep yields in check by repurchasing longer-dated bonds, an earlier boost in the amount of repurchases to $6 billion was smaller than expected, sending yields higher.

At the auction, direct and indirect bidders-the two main parties that generally show up to Treasury auctions-took down almost 96% of the supply. Dealers, who typically buy up the leftover supply at auctions, took just 4.3%, the lowest amount in a year.
On Thursday, $22 billion worth of 30-year Treasury bonds are set to be auctioned, in another test of investor demand.
From here, the bond market's focus will be on August inflation data, with the Producer Price Index release on Thursday and the the Consumer Price Index release on Friday.
"All the long end needs now are benign inflation reads this week and lower oil prices in order to sustain a rally and drop in yields," writes Peter Boockvar, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners CIO.
At current yields, bond investors seem to be sniffing out opportunity.
